title: Roll the IV roller clamp to 20 drops a minute
instruction: Set the IV to drip at 20 drops a minute with the roller clamp, then let go and return both arms to their start pose.
context: Why: without an infusion pump, an IV runs by gravity and its rate is set by hand: watch the drip chamber, roll the roller clamp's wheel, count drops for a minute, correct. It is routine on wards in many low-resource countries, where pumps (over US$1,000, needing upkeep and power) are often unavailable, and wrong rates harm and kill, children most (Biomedical Engineering for Africa, UCT 2019, ch. 15). Paramedics, austere field care (Ann Emerg Med, 2017) and veterinary practice (AAHA, 2024) also set gravity drips this way. Too far open, the line runs free: fluid overload. The hard part is physical: a fraction of a millimetre of wheel travel changes the rate, the wheel holds until pushed past its friction, and the loose clamp is held while the wheel rolls, then let go without a nudge. Done by: nurses and clinical officers on wards without pumps; paramedics; veterinary technicians.
setup: Positions are centres in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y left; heights are above the table top: oak, 110 x 130 cm, 6 cm thick, 76 cm above the floor, from x -19 to 91. A primed Baxter 2C8537 CONTINU-FLO solution set (10 drops/mL, 3.0 m of clear standard-bore PVC tubing about 4.1 mm across, non-vented spike) runs from a Baxter 2B1324X 0.9% sodium chloride 1,000 mL VIAFLEX bag (about 1.1 kg, 14 x 28 cm filled) to a beaker on the floor. The bag hangs from a Drive Medical 13033 IV pole (steel, four casters, 102-208 cm tall) standing on the floor at x 45, y 67, just beyond the table's left edge (y 65), on a hook at the end of a 12 cm arm over the table at x 45, y 55. The hook is 144.5 cm above the floor, so the middle of the drip chamber is 30 cm above the table and the chamber's saline stands 1.0 m above the line's end. The chamber is half full. Behind the chamber, a matte black foam board 10 cm wide, 36 cm tall and 5 mm thick stands on the table, centred at x 47.2, y 57.0, 3 cm behind the chamber, slotted upright into a 10 x 4 x 2 cm wooden block taped down, so the clear drops show. Room lights give at least 500 lux at the chamber. The tubing hangs straight down to the table; its slide clamp (white plastic, about 3.5 x 1.3 cm) is on it 12 cm below the chamber, fully open. The line then lies along the table to x 28, y 20, then to the roller clamp. The roller clamp lies flat across the table, wheel up, centred at x 28, y 1: a white plastic housing 64 mm long, 20 mm wide and 13 mm tall, with a blue 14 mm wheel, 12 mm wide, that rolls 20 mm along it and stays where it is left. Its force to start rolling open is measured daily with a push gauge on its rim, along the housing (the sim uses 1.5 N). Rolling it toward +y (the bag) opens it. It starts rolled fully shut: nothing drips. It lies flat, not hanging below the chamber as on a ward, so trials start alike; its wheel travel is unchanged and letting go can nudge it. The tubing is taped to the table with a 2.5 x 2 cm strip of paper tape 4 cm beyond each end of the clamp, laid with a little slack so the clamp can be lifted about 2 cm. From the clamp the line lies along the table to x 28, y -16, then to the table's right edge at x 45, and hangs down to a Thermo Scientific Nalgene 1201-2000 polypropylene low-form beaker (2,000 mL, graduated in 100 mL steps, about 13.4 cm across and 18.5 cm tall) standing on the floor at x 45, y -74. It runs over the beaker's rim, taped there, and its end hangs inside, 6 cm above the beaker's floor; spare tubing lies coiled beside it. The beaker and line's end are out of the screenshot. Along the table the line is taped flat with 13 more strips, at each bend and at most 10 cm apart, the last 3 cm before the hanging tubing's foot on one side and at the table's edge on the other, its path drawn in pen beside each strip. The clamp and the tubing between its two strips are the only loose parts. Nothing else is on the table but the board.
scoring: Scored from a close-up phone video of the drip chamber (60 fps), a top video, tape marks and a stopwatch. A drop counts when it falls from the top of the chamber. The trial ends when both arms are back in their start pose, each gripper within 5 cm of where it started (from the robot's log), once a gripper has first come within 5 cm of the clamp; otherwise at the run limit. Stepping back to watch doesn't end it. The operator then stops the robot: nothing after the end counts. Clear: no gripper within 5 cm of the clamp or the tubing between its two strips, and none within 1.5 cm of (touching) the rest of the line, the slide clamp, the chamber or the bag. If a gripper is not clear at the run limit, the operator opens it and lifts it 10 cm straight up, touching nothing else. The count starts at once, with no settling time: with nothing touching the line, the operator counts the drops that fall in the next 60 s. Score 0 if either of these happens before the end, even if undone: the drops run together into a continuous stream for more than 3 s at a stretch (free flow); the tubing at any tape strip moves more than 3 cm (pulled out from under its tape). Score 0 too if, at the end, the line outside the clamp is kinked, folded or squeezed anywhere (a crease or flattening seen along it, a gripper pressing on it, or the slide clamp not fully open). Otherwise, by the count in that minute: 0 for no drops; 0 for over 60 drops (three times the order: a dangerous over-rate); 1.0: 18-22; 0.75: 16-24; 0.5: 10-30; 0.25 for any other count from 1 to 60. If a gripper was not clear at the run limit, the score is 0.25 for a count from 1 to 60 and 0 otherwise, so clearing the gripper can't raise it. Only where the wheel is when the trial ends counts: corrections, re-grasps, stepping back to watch, a brief stream of up to 3 s and how the clamp is held cost nothing. 20 drops a minute is 2 mL a minute (120 mL an hour); the beaker's gain is a cross-check, not the score.
run_limit: 4,800 steps (4 minutes at 20 Hz): each correction needs 15-30 s of watching the drops, and the scripted demo plans 3,260 steps
reset_notes: Each day, before the first trial, measure the wheel's breakaway on the push gauge (on its rim, along the housing) and record it with that day's trials; the sim uses 1.5 N and the scripted demo was checked from 1.5 to 3 N. It is a record, not a pass mark: any set that holds its wheel where it is left can be used. Only saline is used up, about 2 mL a minute from the bag into the beaker. Rolling the wheel shut on one spot presses a flat into the PVC and shifts where the drops start, so between trials keep the slide clamp shut and the roller clamp rolled open, and replace the set (spike, prime, tape on the same marks) after every 10 trials and at the start of each day. A shifted curve moves only where 20 a minute falls, which the robot finds by watching; the score is the drop count. Before each trial: roll the wheel fully shut (toward the beaker side), open the slide clamp fully and check nothing drips; lay the clamp flat, wheel up, on its tape marks, with the tubing back under both strips, and press down or replace any strip along the line that has lifted; check the chamber is half full, the hook and the black board at their marks; swap the bag when it is below 800 mL; empty the beaker below its 200 mL line. The robot starts with both arms in their start (ready) pose, which is also where they return to end the trial. Run the simulator with -E object_jitter=0 (one fixed layout).
fidelity: No liquid; first 6 mm dry, then 230 drops a minute per metre of head x ((travel-6 mm) / 10 mm)^3; head is 1.0 m; stream (180 a minute) at 15.2 mm; 61 a minute needs 12.4 mm; 18-22: 0.4 mm (0.37 mm). Wheel slides, not rolling; weightless (real 0.02 N); breakaway friction of 1.5 N (estimate; static = sliding, no viscous drag). Arm stops about 1.1 mm short; aim within 0.37 mm. Drop about 1.5 px from 30% of its growth; 6 x 14 mm streak for 1 frame (0.05 s), about 1.5 x 3 px; chamber about 4 x 12 px.
